speaker: Rory Sutherland
title: Marketing Expert: The Playbook Behind Every Great Campaign | Rory Sutherland
question: In advertising and marketing, why did shifting agencies from media commissions to hourly billing undermine breakthrough creative work?
guest: In the Mad Men era, agency remuneration respected how marketing works because you were paid on commission. If you had a big idea and came up with a campaign that the client spent millions running, you made money from that campaign for years after you conceived it—rather like having royalties on a book. Then media independence came along, so we had to be paid by the hour like lawyers and management consultants, and we've never recovered because it's a catastrophic way to be paid. Marketing is fat-tailed, just like innovation, R&D, pharmaceutical research, and science: five to ten percent of what you do delivers perhaps a hundred and ten percent of the value. Paying people by the hour demands that every quantum of effort be matched to a quantum of value creation in neat proportion. If you have a brilliant idea whose value lasts ten years, you are still held responsible for every unit of cost year by year—you cannot offset current costs against the huge value you created earlier. Ogilvy Australia conceived an idea for a major FMCG company that has made over a billion dollars across a hundred markets over ten years, and the agency made three hundred and fifty thousand Australian dollars. If you cannot claim credit beyond the quarter or financial year in which you had the idea, you systematically underfund breakthrough marketing.

points.core: Marketing returns follow a fat-tailed distribution where rare ideas dominate value.
points.note: Accept: power-law or asymmetric payoffs where a tiny fraction (e.g., 5-10%) of campaigns generate most returns, similar to R&D or drug discovery. Do not credit: generic claims that creativity is unpredictable or hard to measure.

points.core: Hourly billing forces every unit of effort to match proportional output.
points.note: Accept: linear time-and-materials fees pressuring agencies toward predictable, low-variance incremental work rather than high-upside creative bets. Do not credit: vague complaints that hourly billing incentivizes working slowly.

points.core: Removing ongoing royalties prevents agencies from capturing multi-year compounding idea value.
points.note: Accept: losing commission or royalty structures stops agencies from earning recurring upside on multi-year hits or offsetting failed experiments against past breakthroughs. Do not credit: generic claims that agencies are simply underpaid.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Under the commission system, agencies earned a percentage (traditionally 15%) of the media spend, so their income was tied to the scale and success of the campaign rather than to the time spent making it. A great idea that justified a bigger media buy paid off handsomely, and the surplus margin funded top creative talent, speculative thinking, and long gestation of ideas.

Hourly billing changed what agencies sell: time instead of ideas. That had several corrosive effects. A brilliant idea conceived in an afternoon earns less than a mediocre one that takes weeks, so value is decoupled from compensation. Agencies are rewarded for staffing and billable activity, not for outcomes, which favors safe, labor-intensive executions over risky breakthroughs. Client procurement departments could then treat creative work as a commodity, benchmarking and squeezing rates, which shrank margins, pushed work to cheaper junior staff, and eliminated the slack needed for exploration. Finally, the unbundling of media from creative removed the creative agency's stake in the campaign's overall impact.

In short, the incentive shifted from producing big, effective ideas to logging hours efficiently, a point long argued by critics such as Michael Farmer in *Madison Avenue Manslaughter*.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer:
Under the traditional media commission model, agency revenue scaled with campaign success: when a breakthrough idea drove client growth and larger media budgets, the agency shared in the upside. Those margins funded senior talent, deep consumer insight, and speculative creative risk.

Shifting to hourly billing decoupled pay from commercial impact, pricing effort instead of value. Because billable hours reward time spent rather than effectiveness, agencies were penalized for solving problems quickly with a single big idea and incentivized toward labor-intensive volume and endless revisions. Simultaneously, hourly rate cards invited client procurement teams to treat creativity as a commodity, squeezing margins and eliminating the financial slack needed for unbilled exploration and iteration. To stay profitable under rigid scopes, agencies replaced seasoned creatives with cheaper junior staff and pushed high utilization targets that left little room to think. Stripped of media-scale upside and audited on cost efficiency, agencies shifted from bold growth partners into risk-averse vendors delivering safe, predictable output.

noweb.answer:
Shifting from media commissions to hourly billing decoupled agency compensation from market impact and tied it instead to labor inputs, fundamentally misaligning incentives. Under the traditional commission model, agencies shared in a client’s upside: a bold, effective campaign grew sales, expanding media budgets and agency revenue alongside them. Those predictable margins also subsidized creative slack, giving senior talent the freedom to experiment, discard mediocre drafts, and champion risky ideas with clients. A transformative insight conceived in ten minutes was rewarded for its commercial value rather than penalized for its speed.

Hourly billing inverted this dynamic by treating creativity as a commoditized expense policed by corporate procurement. Paying for hours rather than outcomes financially punishes flashes of brilliance while rewarding slow, bloated processes and safe, consensus-driven revisions. To protect margins under relentless rate pressure, agencies replaced expensive, seasoned creatives with cheaper junior staff and obsessed over billable utilization—eliminating the unhurried exploration, creative independence, and risk appetite that breakthrough work demands.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Under the old 15% media commission, agencies were paid as a share of what clients spent running the ads, not for the work of making them. Creative work was effectively bundled in for free, so the agency's interest matched the client's: a big, memorable idea justified bigger media budgets and longer relationships, and nobody counted how many hours a team spent getting there.

From the 1990s onward, procurement departments pushed agencies onto hourly fees and labour-cost-plus models, which pay for effort instead of outcomes. That reverses the incentives. An idea that comes to someone in the shower is worth little on a timesheet, while a mediocre one dragged through months of meetings and revisions pays well, so efficiency and insight are punished and busywork is rewarded. Clients started treating creative work as a cost to cut, negotiating rates down while asking for more deliverables. Agencies answered with leaner, more junior staff, more output and safer work. Shared upside in the client's success was replaced by a supplier selling labour, so the time and risk-taking that breakthrough ideas need had no economic home. Critics such as Michael Farmer and Rory Sutherland have argued that this is why the industry turned commodity-like and creatively timid.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer:
Under the traditional 15% media commission model, an agency’s financial upside was tied to the scale and success of its work: a breakthrough campaign drove business growth, encouraging clients to buy more media and rewarding the agency for asymmetric creative value. Shifting to hourly billing severed that link by pegging revenue to labor inputs rather than commercial outcomes.

Because breakthrough ideas rarely correlate with time spent—a transformative insight can take an hour, while mediocre work can take months—hourly billing perversely penalizes speed, seniority, and originality. Agencies earn more by dragging out processes, multiplying meetings, and staffing accounts with layers of billable junior talent than by delivering a single bold concept quickly. Meanwhile, billing by the hour invited procurement departments to treat creativity as a commoditized expense, scrutinizing rates and timesheets instead of business impact. Facing capped margins and high downside risk if a daring idea failed, agencies naturally pivoted toward safe, predictable, high-volume deliverables that reliably filled hours rather than swinging for genuine creative breakthroughs.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Media commissions paid agencies a percentage of what clients spent placing ads. That revenue gave agencies room to fund speculative ideas, explore several directions, and absorb the cost of work that went nowhere. Hourly billing put each round of exploration against a client’s budget, making it harder to justify time spent on an idea that might fail.

It also tied the agency’s revenue to the time a campaign took to produce. A breakthrough idea found in an afternoon could earn the agency less than a conventional campaign that took weeks. Clients had reason to cap hours, and agencies had reason to favor work they could estimate and bill for. Breakthrough creative work often depends on the freedom to follow an uncertain idea before anyone can say what it will be worth.
